en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daoyi of Mazu in Jiangxi.
Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi was a native of Shifang County in Hanzhou. His surname was Ma. He left the household life at Luohan Temple in his home district.
His appearance was extraordinary: he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger; he could extend his tongue beyond his nose, and there were two wheels beneath each of his feet.

Dongshan Liangjie was tonsured at the age of youth by Master Tang of Zizhou. He received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he practiced meditative concentration at the Chuanfa Temple on Mount Heng.
There he met Master Rang, who recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by sitting in meditation? The Master replied, "I hope to become a Buddha.

Master Rang then took a brick and began rubbing it against a stone. (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the full dialogue continues with Master Rang asking why he is polishing a brick to make a mirror, to which Dongshan replies that he is polishing a brick to make a Buddha.)
Before the hut, Mazu was polishing a tile. The Master asked, "What are you doing, polishing a tile? Letting said, "I am polishing it to make a mirror.
The Master said, "How can polishing a tile produce a mirror? Letting said, "If polishing a tile cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?
The Master asked, "What then would do so? Letting replied, "It is like a cow pulling a cart: if the cart does not move, shall one beat the cart or shall one beat the cow?"

The Master had no reply. Letting further said, "Are you practicing seated meditation, or are you practicing sitting as a Buddha? If you are practicing seated meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down.
If you are practicing sitting as a Buddha, a Buddha has no fixed form. Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha;
if you cling to the form of sitting, you have not realized its principle. Upon hearing these instructions, the Master was as if...
He drank the *amṛta* (clarified butter) and, after prostrating, asked: "How should one apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?
Nanyue Ruan said: "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground is like sowing seeds; my teaching of the essential Dharma is like the moisture from heaven.
Because your conditions have converged, you shall perceive the Way. He asked again: "The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be perceived? Ruan said: "The Mind-Ground..."
"The Dharma-eye can see the Way; it is the same with the signless samādhi. The Master asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?
Huairang replied, "If one sees the Way through arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing, that is not seeing the Way. Listen to my verse: [Verse follows]
The ground of the mind contains all seeds; when it encounters moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless; what could be destroyed, and what could be formed?

Upon receiving this instruction, the Master attained enlightenment, and his mind became transcendent. He served [the Sixth Patriarch] for ten years, and day by day he grew more profound and mysterious. Initially, the Sixth Patriarch said to Huairang:
"The prophecy of Prajñātāra of the Western Heaven states that from beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample others to death."
The people of the world generally refer to the Master as such. He deferred to six disciples, yet it was only the Master who secretly received the Mind-Seal (Citta-mudrā).
Initially, he moved from Mount Fotuo in Jianyang to Linchuan; subsequently, he went to Mount Gonggong in Nankang.

During the Dali era, he registered his name at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling. At that time, the Regional Commander Lu Sigong, having heard of his reputation and admired him, personally received the [Dharma] lineage from him.
The essence of the matter was this: consequently, scholars from the four quarters gathered at his seat like clouds.

When Master Ràng heard that the Teacher had begun to propagate the Dharma in Jiangxi, he asked the assembly, "Does Dào-yī preach the Dharma for the community? The assembly replied, "He has already preached the Dharma for the community.
Ràng said, "But no one has brought back any news of it yet. He then dispatched a monk there with the instruction: "When he ascends the hall, simply—"
The Master asked, "What do you say? Wait until he has something to say, and then remember it. The monk followed these instructions and went to ask him.
The Master said, "Since the time of chaos, for thirty years, there has been no lack of salt and sauce. When the monk returned, he reported this to Huairang, who approved of it.
The Master had one hundred and thirty-nine入室 disciples (入室弟子), each of whom became a patriarch in their own region, continuing his transformation of beings without end.

In the first month of the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Master ascended Mount Shimen in Jianchang and was walking in meditation amidst the woods when he saw that the caves and ravines were level and open.
He said to his attendant, "This withered body of mine shall return to this place next month.
Having finished speaking, he turned back. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness. The head of the monastery asked, "How is the Master’s health these days?"
The Master said: "Buddha of the Sunny Face, Buddha of the Moonly Face. On the first day of the second month, he bathed, sat in the full-lotus posture, and entered nirvana.
During the Yuanhe era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Daji, and his stupa was named Dazhuangyan (Great Adornment).
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, believe each that your own mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle, the single mind, so as to cause you all to attain awakening.
He further cited the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the ground of the minds of sentient beings, fearing that you might be deluded and lack faith."
This Dharma of the one mind is possessed by each and every being. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core principle and "no-gate" as its dharma-gate.
Now, those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no separate mind.
Do not grasp at good, do not abandon evil, and rely upon neither of the two extremes of purity and defilement. Realize that the nature of transgression is empty.
Moment-to-moment, they are ungraspable because they lack intrinsic nature. Therefore, the three realms are mind-only. The myriad phenomena and all things are sealed by this single Dharma.
Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind; the mind does not exist as a mind of its own accord, but exists only in dependence upon form.
You need only speak according to the occasion; whether in terms of phenomena or principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
It is the same with the fruit of the Bodhi path: that which arises within the mind is immediately termed "form. Because one knows form to be empty, arising is non-arising.
If you understand this meaning, you may then dress and eat according to the occasion, nourishing the sacred embryo and passing the time spontaneously. Furthermore—
"What is it? You have received my instruction; listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion; Bodhi is likewise only tranquility.
When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, that which arises is precisely non-arising.'"
A monk asked, "What is the cultivation of the Way? The Master said, "The Way does not belong to cultivation. If one says it can be cultivated, then once it is accomplished, it will still perish;
this is the same as the Śrāvakas. If one says it cannot be cultivated, then one is the same as an ordinary person. The monk asked again, "By what kind of insight can one attain the Way?
The Master said, "The self-nature is originally complete. It is simply a matter of not being obstructed by matters of good and evil. This is called..."
A practitioner of the Way who takes up the good and abandons evil, or who contemplates emptiness and enters meditative concentration, still belongs to the realm of conditioned activity.

If they further pursue it outwardly, they will become increasingly estranged and distant from the truth. Simply exhaust the mental scope of the triple world; the single thought of deluded mind is itself the root of birth and death within the triple world.
If one simply lacks even a single thought, the root of birth and death is eliminated, and one attains the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma King.
O Jewel, for immeasurable kalpas, the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings—characterized by flattery, crookedness, deceit, falsehood, pride, and arrogance—have coalesced into a single entity.
Therefore, a sutra says: "This body is merely composed of a multitude of dharmas; when it arises, only dharmas arise; when it ceases, only dharmas cease.
When these dharmas arise, they do not say 'I arise'; when they cease, they do not say 'I cease. This applies to every preceding and succeeding thought."
In the midst of mindfulness, each moment of thought does not wait for the next; each moment is quiescent and extinguished. This is called the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
It encompasses all phenomena, just as hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean and are collectively called "ocean water.
Abiding in this single flavor, it subsumes all flavors; abiding in the great ocean, it merges all currents. It is like a person bathing in the great ocean who uses only one [drop].

Cutting through the water. Thus, while Śrāvakas awaken from delusion and ordinary beings are deluded regarding awakening, the Śrāvakas do not know that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally devoid of stages, causes, effects, or hierarchical ranks.
They harbor mental constructs and false imaginings, cultivating causes and realizing fruits, and abide in empty samādhis for eighty thousand or twenty thousand kalpas;
though they have attained awakening, once awakened they fall back into delusion. To the various Bodhisattvas, these states appear as painful as being in hell.
To sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence is to fail to see the Buddha-nature.

If, however, a sentient being of superior capacity suddenly encounters the guidance of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and attains realization in a single word, they will not have to traverse the various stages and positions, but will instead achieve sudden awakening to their original nature. Thus, a sutra says:
"Ordinary people possess a mind that turns back and forth, whereas the śrāvakas do not. This is said in contrast to delusion; since there is fundamentally no delusion, there is no need for awakening.
Even awakening is not established. All sentient beings, from immeasurable kalpas past, have never departed from the samādhi of the dharma-nature;

they have long remained within the samādhi of the dharma-nature. Whether putting on clothes or eating food, speaking or responding in conversation, employing the six sense faculties, or performing any activity whatsoever—all these are entirely the dharma-nature.
Failing to understand how to return to the source, they follow names and pursue appearances; deluded sentiments arise falsely, and they create various karmic seeds.
Regarding the various karmas: if you can, for even a single thought-moment, reflect back upon yourself, your entire being will be the sacred mind.
You all must each realize your own mind; do not merely memorize my words. Even if you were able to explain as many principles as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, your mind would not increase;
even if you cannot explain them, your mind would not decrease. To be able to speak it is your mind; to be unable to speak it is also your mind. Thus...

Even the manifestation of divided bodies and the emission of light, and the display of the eighteen transformations, are not as good as returning my dead ashes to me. Dead ashes that have been soaked are powerless;

this is a metaphor for the Śrāvakas who falsely cultivate causes and realize fruits. Dead ashes that have not been soaked are powerful; this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattvas whose path and practice are fully matured and untainted by any evils.
If one were to explain the Tathāgata’s provisional teachings of the Tripiṭaka, one might speak for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is not exhausted; it is like a hook and chain that never breaks. If one awakens to the sacred mind, there is nothing else remaining. [The Master] stood for a long time and said, "Be careful.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Way does not require cultivation; one need only avoid defilement. What constitutes defilement? It is simply the presence of the mind of birth and death."
All deliberate activity and directed striving are defilements. If you wish to directly realize the Way, the ordinary mind is itself the Way.

What is meant by the "ordinary mind"? It is without deliberate activity; it is without right or wrong; it is without grasping or rejecting; it is without annihilationism or eternalism; it is without the ordinary and without the holy.

The Sūtra says: "It is not the practice of ordinary beings; it is not the practice of sages; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas. Indeed, at this very moment—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;

whether responding to sentient beings or interacting with others—all of it is the Way. The Way is itself the Dharma-realm. Even the wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges do not transcend the Dharma-realm.
If it were otherwise, how could one speak of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground? How could one speak of the Inexhaustible Lamp?
All phenomena (*dharma*) are mental phenomena; all names are mental names. All myriad dharmas arise from the mind;
the mind is the root of all myriad dharmas. As a sutra says: "One who knows the mind and reaches its source is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Whether in terms of names or meanings, all dharmas are equal—pure, singular, and unmixed. If one attains this within the gates of the teachings, it follows accordingly...

At that time, sovereignty is established. The entire dharma-realm is this very dharma-realm. If one establishes true suchness, all is true suchness. If one establishes principle, all dharmas are entirely principle.
If one establishes phenomena, all dharmas are entirely phenomena. Taking one as the leader, the thousand follow; there is no distinction between principle and phenomena.
All are wondrous functions; there is no separate principle apart from them. This is entirely due to the turning of the mind. It is like a metaphor...
Just as there may be many reflections of the moon, yet the true moon has no multiplicity; there may be many waters in various sources, yet the nature of water has no multiplicity;

there may be many myriad phenomena arrayed throughout the universe, yet empty space has no multiplicity; so too, there may be many ways of explaining the principle, yet the principle itself has no multiplicity.
Unobstructed wisdom is not manifold; its various manifestations are all derived from the one mind.
It can be established, and it can be swept away—all of this is its wondrous function, and all of this is one's own self. There is no place of establishment apart from the Truth;
the place of establishment is itself the Truth. All of this is the substance of one's own self. If it were not so, who else could it be? All dharmas are thus.
The Buddha-dharma: all dharmas are themselves liberation; liberation is itself suchness (*tathatā*). No dharma transcends suchness.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, all are inconceivable functions that do not depend upon time or season. As the Sūtra says: "In whatever place [one dwells], there is a Buddha.
A Buddha is a Capable Sage (*śakya-muni*); possessing wisdom and a skillful nature, he is able to shatter all [obstructions].
Sentient beings are freed from the net of doubt and the bonds of existence and non-existence. Both the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted; both person and phenomena are empty.
One turns toward that which is peerless, transcending all calculation and measure. In all actions there is no obstruction; affairs and principle are simultaneously penetrated.

Like clouds arising in the sky, appearing suddenly and then vanishing without a trace, it is like drawing patterns upon water—neither born nor extinguished. This is Great Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-śānti-nirvāṇa*).

When enveloped by afflictions, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*; when free from these envelopments, it is called the pure *dharmakāya*. This *dharmakāya* is infinite; its essence neither increases nor decreases.
It can manifest as large or small, as square or round, appearing in forms that respond to sentient beings like the moon reflected in water. Its functioning flows on ceaselessly.

It does not establish roots, it does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and it does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The conditioned is the function of the unconditioned, and the unconditioned is the support of the conditioned.

Because it does not abide in that support, it is said to be "like space, having no support. This refers to the meaning of the mind’s arising and ceasing, and the meaning of the mind as suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the mind as suchness: it is like a bright mirror reflecting images; the mirror is a metaphor for the mind, and the images...
This illustrates all phenomena (*dharmas*). If the mind grasps at phenomena, it is externally involved; this is the meaning of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions.
Not grasping at phenomena is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). Śrāvakas hear and see the Buddha-nature; Bodhisattvas see the Buddha-nature with their eyes.

To thoroughly realize that these are non-dual is called the nature of equality. This nature has no difference, yet its functions differ: in delusion it is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while in awakening...
To act in accordance with wisdom is to be enlightened; to act in accordance with phenomena is to be deluded. Delusion is to be confused regarding one's own original mind;
enlightenment is to awaken to one's own original nature. Once awakened, one is forever awakened and shall never again fall into delusion—just as when the sun rises, it cannot coexist with darkness.
The sun of wisdom rises; it does not coexist with the darkness of afflictions. When one thoroughly understands the mind and its objects, delusive thoughts do not arise.

Since delusive thoughts do not arise, this is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It has existed from the beginning and exists now; it does not depend on the cultivation of the path or sitting in meditation.
This non-cultivation and non-sitting is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata. If you can now see this principle as it truly is, [you have attained it].
Do not create any further karma; let your life pass according to your lot. With but one robe and one patchwork cloak, let them accompany you in sitting and rising.

Let your cultivation of the precepts increase its fragrance and accumulate pure karma. If you can simply act in this way, why worry that you will not attain success? I have stood for a long time; farewell to all, take care.
Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were attending the Patriarch while enjoying the moon. The Patriarch asked, "At this very moment, how is it? Xitang said, "It is precisely right for making offerings.
Baizhang said, "It is precisely right for practicing the Way. Nanquan shook his sleeves and departed. The Patriarch said, "The Sutras enter the Canon;
Zen returns to the Sea. Only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world. (Xitang is "Zang," Baizhang is "Hai," and Nanquan is "Yuan.")
When Nanquan was serving congee to the assembly of monks, the Patriarch asked, "What is that in the bucket?
Nanquan said, "Old man, shut your mouth and stop talking like that! Thereupon, the Patriarch ceased.
Baizhang asked, "What is the essential purport of the Buddha? The Patriarch replied, "It is precisely where you let go of body and life.
When Dazhu first visited the Patriarch, the Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. The Patriarch asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here?
He replied, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "You neglect your own precious treasury."
"What is the point of abandoning your home and wandering about? Here, I have not a single thing. What Buddhist Dharma do you seek?
Zhuhui then prostrated and asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Huihai himself? The Patriarch said, "That which is asking me right now is your own precious treasury.
It is fully complete with everything; there is nothing lacking. Its use is sovereign—why rely on anything else?"

Seeking it outwardly, he recognized his own original mind beneath the Master’s words; this was not achieved through intellectual cognition. He prostrated himself with great joy and gratitude, serving as a disciple for six years.

Later, upon returning home, he composed the *Tunwu rudao yaomen lun* (Treatise on the Essential Gate of Sudden Enlightenment for Entering the Way) in one fascicle. When the Patriarch saw it, [he approved].
He addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a great pearl—perfectly round, luminous, and penetrating; it is free and at ease, with no place for obstruction.
Letang Fahui Chan Master asked the Patriarch, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Patriarch said, "Lower your voice and come closer. Fahui then stepped forward. The Patriarch gave him a slap on the cheek and said, "Six ears do not share a secret. The next day...
The next day, when the assembly had gathered, Xuansha still entered the Dharma Hall and said, "I request the Master to speak. Nanquan said, "Go for now;

wait until I ascend the hall, and I will come out to provide testimony for you. Xuansha then attained realization and said, "I thank the Great Assembly for their testimony," whereupon he circumambulated the Dharma Hall once and departed.
One day, Chan Master Ledu Weijian was sitting in meditation behind the Dharma Hall. When the Patriarch saw him, he blew into Jian’s ears twice.
Jian rose from his meditative absorption and, seeing it was the Patriarch, returned once more to his concentration. The Patriarch went back to his quarters and ordered an attendant:
He took a bowl of tea and gave it to Jian, but Jian paid him no heed and simply returned to the hall.
As for Chan Master Shigong Huizang, he originally made his living as a hunter and detested seeing śramaṇas; thus, while pursuing a herd of deer, he encountered one.

As he was passing in front of the Patriarch’s hermitage, the Patriarch went out to meet him. Baizhang asked, "Did you see the deer pass by, Master? The Patriarch replied, "Who are you? He said, "A hunter.
The Patriarch asked, "Are you skilled at archery? He said, "I am. The Patriarch asked, "How many deer can you shoot with a single arrow?
He said, "One arrow shoots one deer. The Patriarch said, "Then you do not understand archery. He said, "But you, Master, must understand archery."
"No," the Patriarch said. "Do you understand archery? He replied, "How many does the Master shoot with a single arrow? The Patriarch said, "With one arrow, I shoot a whole flock.
He said, "Since all life is equally precious, why shoot a whole flock? The Patriarch said, "If you already know this, why do you not shoot yourself?
He replied, "If you were to command me to shoot myself, there would be no place to begin. The Patriarch said, "This fellow has been without [awakening] for kalpas on end."
He clarified that his afflictions were now suddenly stilled. At that time, Huìzàng discarded his bow and arrows and cut off his own hair with a knife, entering the monastic order under the Patriarch.
One day, while he was performing chores in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked him, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am tending the ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you tend it?
He said, "Whenever it enters the grass, I pull it back by the nostrils. The Patriarch said, "My son..."
Truly tending the ox.
A monk asked the Patriarch, "I pray the Master will transcend the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations, and directly point out to me the meaning of the Westward Journey.
The Patriarch said, "I have no mind for this today; go ask Zhizang. The monk then went and asked Zhizang. Zhizang—
The monk said, "Why do you not go ask your preceptor? The monk said, "The Preceptor sent me here to ask you, Venerable.
Cang rubbed his head with his hand and said, "Today my head aches. You should go ask Brother Hai. The monk went again to ask Hai. Hai said, "I, for my part, do not understand this.
The monk then reported this to the Patriarch (Nanyue Huairang). The Patriarch said, "Cang’s head is white; Hai’s is black."
Touhei. One day, while following the Patriarch on a walk, Chan Master Magu Baiche asked, "What is Great Nirvana?
The Patriarch said, "Hurry! Baiche asked, "Hurry for what? The Patriarch said, "Look at the water."
Chan Master Fachang of Mount Daimei first visited the Patriarch [Huineng] and asked, "What is the Buddha? The Patriarch replied, "The mind itself is the Buddha.
At these words, Chang attained great enlightenment. Later, he resided on Mount Daimei. When the Patriarch heard that the Master was living in the mountains, he sent a monk to him with the question:
"Upon meeting Master Ma, what did you receive that caused you to settle here on this mountain? Chang said, "Master Ma..."
"My teaching is that 'the mind itself is Buddha,' and I have always dwelt in this very place. The monk said, "Master Ma’s Dharma has recently become different.
[Baizhang] asked, "In what way is it different? The monk said, "Recently he has also said, 'Neither mind nor Buddha. [Baizhang] said, "I have always said..."
"This old fellow will continue to delude people until the very end of time. Let you maintain 'neither mind nor Buddha' as you wish;
I shall simply maintain 'this very mind is Buddha. When the monk returned and related this to the Patriarch, the Patriarch said, "The plum has ripened."
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou went to visit the Patriarch. The Patriarch observed that his appearance was magnificent and his voice resonant like a bell, and he said, "Aloft is the Buddha Hall;
within it, there is no Buddha. Wuye prostrated himself and knelt to ask, "I have roughly exhausted the essential meanings of the literature of the Three Vehicles.
I have often heard in the Chan gate that 'the very mind is Buddha,' yet I truly have not been able to comprehend this. The Patriarch replied, "It is precisely because you have not comprehended it."
"The very ground of the mind is it; there is nothing else. Again, Huaiye asked, "What is the patriarch’s secret transmission of the mind-seal upon his coming from the West?
The Patriarch said, "Virtuous One, you are quite busy right now. Go for now and come back at another time. As soon as Huaiye had stepped out, the Patriarch called to him.
"Virtuous One," said Jue Huishou. The Patriarch asked, "What is it? At this, Jue attained realization and prostrated.
The Patriarch said, "This dull-witted fellow! Why do you prostrate?"
Deng Yinfeng took his leave of the Patriarch (Nanquan). The Patriarch asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am going to Shitou. The Patriarch said, "The path at Shitou is slippery.
He replied, "Carrying my staff and wood with me, I perform my play wherever the stage appears," and he departed.

As soon as he arrived at Shitou, he circumambulated the meditation seat once, struck his monk’s staff once, and asked, "What is your fundamental teaching? Shitou said, "Heaven! Heaven! Yinfeng was speechless and turned back.
Upon his return, he reported this to the Patriarch. The Patriarch said, "Go back again. When he says, 'Heaven! Heaven! you must then let out two sighs.

Huifeng went again and followed the previous instructions exactly. When the Master asked the same question, Huiming let out two sighs. Huifeng remained speechless once more. On his return, he reported this to the Patriarch.
The Patriarch said, "I told you that the path at Shitou is slippery."
One day, as Xuansha was pushing a cart, his teacher, Mazu, sat on the road with his legs extended. Xuansha said, "I request that you withdraw your feet, Master.
Mazu replied, "Once extended, they are not withdrawn. Xuansha said, "Once advanced, there is no retreating," and he pushed the cart over him, injuring Mazu’s feet.
He returned to the Dharma Hall and, holding an axe, said, "The one who just now came out and damaged the old monk's feet, step forward!
Feng then stepped forth and extended his neck before the Patriarch. The Patriarch then set down the axe.
When Master Shijiu first visited the Patriarch, the Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Shijiu replied, "I have come from Wujiao.
The Patriarch asked, "What sayings or phrases has Wujiao been teaching lately? Shijiu replied, "How many people remain utterly bewildered by this?
The Patriarch said, "Setting aside for a moment their bewilderment—how about that single phrase of silent stillness? Shijiu then stepped forward three paces. The Patriarch said, "I have..."
"Seven blows! Sent to strike the mortar: do you still find it sweet? The mortar replied, "The Master shall eat first; I shall find it sweet later.
He then returned to Wujiao.
Master Liang went to visit the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked him, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sutras and śāstras;

is this true? Liang replied, "I dare not say so. The Patriarch said, "With what do you lecture? Liang said, "I lecture with the mind. The Patriarch said, "The mind is like a skilled performer, and the intellect is like the conductor of the performance;
how can such things understand the sutras? Liang raised his voice and said, "If the mind cannot lecture, then [the self] is empty..."
The Master said, "Can emptiness (*ākāśa*) preach? Dazhu replied, "In fact, it is emptiness that can preach. Huiliang did not accept this and departed.
As he was descending the steps, the Master called out, "Preceptor! Huiliang turned his head and was suddenly and completely enlightened;
he then prostrated himself. The Master said, "Why does this dull-witted monk prostrate? Huiliang returned to the monastery and told the assembly: "The sutras and treatises I have preached..."
This means that there was neither person nor attainment. Today, having been subjected to a single question by Master Ma, his lifelong efforts melted away like ice and crumbled like tiles.
He went straight into the Western Mountains, leaving no further trace.
When the Old Monk Shuilao of Hongzhou first visited the Patriarch, he asked, "What is the very meaning of the coming from the West?
The Patriarch said, "Prostrate yourself. As soon as the Old Monk prostrated, the Patriarch gave him a kick. The Old Monk attained great enlightenment;

rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and the immeasurable subtle meanings all reside within this one kick!"
On the tip of a single hair, he immediately recognized the source; he then bowed and withdrew. Later, he told the assembly:
"Ever since I took one bite from Master Ma’s kick, I have been laughing without end until this very day."
Master Pang asked the Patriarch, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
The Patriarch replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River with a single draught, and then I will tell you.

He asked the Patriarch again, "The person who is fundamentally unobscured—please, Master, cast your eyes high. The Patriarch looked straight down at him. Master Pang said, "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it."

He attained the wondrous. The Master went straight up to look at him, whereupon the scholar prostrated himself. The Patriarch returned to his quarters, and the scholar followed him in, saying, "Just now, my cleverness turned into clumsiness.
He then asked, "As for the saying, 'Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-bushel boat'—what is the principle behind this?
The Patriarch replied, "In this place there is neither water nor boat; why speak of sinews and bones?"
A monk asked, "Why did the Master say 'this very mind is Buddha'? The Patriarch said, "To stop a small child's crying.

The monk asked, "What about when the crying has stopped? The Patriarch said, "Neither mind nor Buddha. The monk asked, "If someone other than these two types of people comes, how do you instruct them?
The Patriarch said, "I tell him, 'It is not a thing. The monk asked, "What if someone who is already among those [who have realized this] should come?"
The Patriarch said, "First, let him realize the Great Way.
He asked, "What is the meaning of the West? The Patriarch replied, "Right now, what is this meaning?"
A monk asked, "How can one attain accord with the Way? The Patriarch said, "I have long been out of accord with the Way. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Patriarch struck him and said, "If I did not strike you, people everywhere would laugh at me."
There was a junior master named Danyuan who, upon returning from his pilgrimage, drew a circle before the Patriarch, prostrated himself upon it, and then stood up.
The Patriarch said, "Do you not wish to become a Buddha? He replied, "I do not know how to press my eyes. The Patriarch said, "I am not as good as you.
The junior master remained silent.

There was a monk who, before the Patriarch, made four lines on the ground: the top line was long and the three bottom lines were short. He said, "One must not say that one line is long and three lines are short;
one must transcend the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations. I beg the Master to answer me.
The Patriarch then drew a single line on the ground and said, "One must not speak of long or short. My answer to you is complete."
The Patriarch ordered a monk to deliver a letter to Venerable Qian of Mount Jing. In the letter, he drew a perfect circle.
As soon as Mount Jing opened it and saw it, he took up a brush and placed a single dot within the circle. Later, a monk reported this to National Teacher Huizhong, who said:
Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma.
A lecturer-monk came and asked, "I wonder, what Dharma does the Zen school transmit and uphold? The Patriarch, in turn, asked, "What Dharma do you, O Lecturer, transmit and uphold?
The monk replied, "I am fortunate enough to have lectured on more than twenty volumes of sutras and treatises. The Patriarch said, "Is this not like a lion..."
The Master said, "I dare not. Nanyue made a sound of sighing. The Master said, "This is the Dharma. Nanyue asked, "What Dharma is this?
The Master said, "It is the Dharma of the lion emerging from its cave. Nanyue then remained silent. The Master said, "This, too, is the Dharma."
The Patriarch asked, “What kind of Dharma is this? The Master replied, “The Dharma of the lion in its den. The Patriarch asked, “Neither coming out nor entering—what kind of Dharma is that?
The Master was speechless. He then took his leave and stepped out the door. The Patriarch called out, “Master! The Master turned his head; the Patriarch said:
"What is it? The Master remained silent. The Patriarch said, "This dull-witted monk.
The Provincial Commissioner of Lianzhou asked, "Is it right to eat meat and drink wine, or is it not? The Patriarch replied, "If you eat, it is the official's salary;
if you do not eat, it is the official's merit."
Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan first visited Shitou and asked, "I have a rough understanding of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.
I have often heard it said in the South that one directly points to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha, yet I truly do not understand this clearly.
I humbly hope that the Master will compassionately provide me with instruction. Shitou replied, "It cannot be attained by such means, nor can it be attained by not such means. Such..."
"Neither 'so' nor 'not so'—both are inadmissible. What do you say to this? Shanshan was at a loss for a response.

Baizhang said, "Your karmic conditions do not lie here. Go instead to the place of Master Ma. Shanshan followed these instructions, paid his respects to the Patriarch (Nanyue Huairang), and again posed his former question.
The Patriarch said, "There are times when I instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink; there are times when I do not instruct them to raise their eyebrows and blink."
"Sometimes one who raises his eyebrows and blinks his eyes is it; sometimes one who raises his eyebrows and blinks his eyes is not it.
What do you say to this? At these words, Shanshan attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself?"
Mount said, "I have been at Shitou’s place like a mosquito on an iron ox. The Patriarch said, "Since it is so for you, protect and maintain it well yourself.
He served him for three years. One day, the Patriarch asked him, "What is your realization these days?
Mount replied, "The skin and flesh have fallen away entirely; there is only the single reality. The Patriarch said, "This is what you have attained."
This may be called "harmonizing with the essence of the mind" and "extending it through the four limbs. Since this is so, bring me three strips of bamboo and bind my belly;
I shall go to dwell on a mountain wherever I find one. Baizhang said, "Who are you that dares to speak of dwelling on a mountain?"
The Patriarch said, "It is not so. There has never been one who constantly travels without abiding, nor one who constantly abides without traveling.
To seek benefit is to gain no benefit; to seek to act is to do nothing. You should become a vessel for others; do not remain here for long. Mañjuśrī then took his leave of the Patriarch.
Chan Master Danxia Tianran visited the Patriarch for a second time. Without even having paid his respects, he entered the monks’ hall and sat astride the neck of the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni).
The assembly was struck with astonishment and immediately informed the Patriarch. The Patriarch entered the hall in person to look at him and said, "My son is indeed 'Natural' (Tianran).
Danxia then descended from the ground, prostrated himself, and said, "I thank the Master for bestowing my Dharma name. For this reason, he was named Tianran.
When Chan Master Huilang of Tanzhou first visited the Patriarch, the Patriarch asked, "What do you seek by coming here? He replied, "I seek the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The Patriarch said, "The Buddha has no knowledge or vision; knowledge and vision are but demons. Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Heng.
The Patriarch said, "Since you have come from Mount Heng, you have not yet recognized the essential heart of Caoxi. You should return there immediately; it is not fitting for you to go elsewhere."
The Patriarch asked a monk, “Where have you come from? He replied, “From Hunan. The Patriarch said, “Is the water in Dong Lake full yet? He replied, “Not yet.
The Patriarch said, “After all this time of rain, it is still not full. (Daowu said, “It is full. Yunyan said, “It is limpid and deep.
Dongshan said, “In what kalpa has it ever been lacking?”)
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi
